opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to separate two things people often mix together: progress in benchmark numbers, and progress in the underlying ability to learn. Benchmarks saturate all the time. A score going from 85 to 88 can look like slowing down, but often the benchmark has just stopped measuring what matters. So I don't read too much into curves on fixed leaderboards.

What I look at more is: how efficiently does a model pick up something genuinely new? If you give it a new domain, a new tool, a new kind of task it hasn't really seen, how much data, how much feedback, how much compute does it need to get good? If that cost keeps falling, learning ability is still improving, even if headline numbers look flat.

The second signal is whether new training methods keep unlocking qualitatively new behavior. Pretraining scaling gave us one big wave. Then reinforcement learning and reasoning gave another, where models could think longer and solve problems they couldn't before. The question for me is whether we keep finding these new axes. Diminishing returns on one axis is normal and expected. The real slowdown would be if we stopped finding new axes.

The third thing is the length and complexity of tasks a model can carry through on its own. Can it work for minutes, then hours, then days on something, recover from its own mistakes, and keep improving from what happens along the way? That kind of long-horizon, self-correcting learning is much closer to what we actually care about, and I'd say we're still early there, so there's a lot of room.

So my honest view: on some narrow measures it can look like things are plateauing, but when I look at learning efficiency, new methods, and how far models can go autonomously, I don't think we're slowing down yet. The bottleneck is shifting, from data and compute toward how we design environments and feedback for the model to learn from. That's where I think the next real progress comes from.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning efficiency and new training methods, but does not say that getting models to learn a task requires less ingenuity than before.

r002.rationale: It mentions designing environments and feedback for learning, but does not identify environments as a form of data.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't judge it by looking at benchmarks going up or down, because benchmarks saturate for reasons that have little to do with learning ability. If you only look at MMLU or whatever the current leaderboard is, you'll always conclude things are slowing down, because any fixed test gets solved and then stops being informative.

What I actually look at is the relationship between what a model can do and how much supervision it needed to get there. Learning ability, to me, is about efficiency: how many examples, how much human feedback, how much hand-designed structure does it take for the model to acquire a new capability? If every new capability still requires a team of people to curate a dataset and design a reward for it, then the model isn't really learning, we're learning on its behalf. Progress is slowing down in a meaningful sense when the ratio of human effort to new capability stops improving.

The second thing I look at is generalization across environments. When I was working on agents, the thing that mattered wasn't whether the model solved the environment we trained it on, it was whether the behaviors transferred to something we hadn't anticipated. A model that gets better at one task per unit of training is doing something very different from a model that gets better at a family of tasks it has never seen. If we're only seeing the first kind of improvement, that's a signal the underlying learning isn't getting stronger, we're just pouring more into the same bucket.

And the third thing, which is maybe more philosophical, is whether the bottleneck has shifted. For a long time the bottleneck was the model: it simply couldn't do the thing. Now, for many tasks, the bottleneck is the environment and the evaluation. We don't know how to specify what we want, or how to build a world where the model can practice it. When the bottleneck moves from the model to our ability to define problems, that doesn't mean learning ability has plateaued. It means we've run out of good questions to ask, which is a very different kind of slowdown, and in some ways a more interesting one.

So if someone asks me "is it slowing down," I'd push back on the framing a little. Per-benchmark progress always slows down. The question that actually matters is whether we're getting more capability per unit of human input, and whether that capability transfers. On those two axes I don't think we've seen the curve bend yet. But I do think we're in a period where the limiting factor is increasingly on our side rather than the model's, and that's what people are mistaking for a slowdown.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the bottleneck is increasingly on the human side, but does not report that getting models to learn a task now takes less ingenuity than before.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses training and transfer across environments, but does not identify environments themselves as a form of data for learning.

astra-6.text:
I think we first have to separate two things: whether benchmark scores are improving more slowly, and whether models’ ability to learn is improving more slowly. Those aren’t necessarily the same. A benchmark can become saturated, or it can measure a fairly narrow skill, so a flatter curve doesn’t tell us much by itself.

For learning ability, I would ask: when you give a model a new task, how much experience does it need to get better? Can it use feedback to correct a mistake? And does what it learns transfer to another task, or does it only help with that particular example? Ideally, we would compare those things across generations under similar resource constraints.

There’s also a distinction between learning during training and learning while doing a task. A model might have more knowledge because it has seen more data, but still struggle to improve through interaction with an environment. So I wouldn’t judge this just by how impressive its first answer is. I’d look at the trajectory: after ten attempts, or a hundred attempts, does it become meaningfully more capable?

If that trajectory stops improving across a broad range of genuinely new tasks, then I’d take the slowdown argument much more seriously. Otherwise, we may just be seeing the limits of how we measure progress.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses how much experience models need to improve, but does not say that getting models to learn tasks now requires less ingenuity than before.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions learning through interaction with an environment, but does not identify environments as a form of data for learning.

sol-6.1.text:
我觉得首先要区分，我们说的“学习能力”到底是什么。是预训练时，从更多数据和算力中学到知识的能力，还是在一个具体任务里，根据反馈不断改进的能力？这两件事不一定同步。

如果只看一些固定的 benchmark，分数涨得越来越慢，并不能直接说明学习能力在放缓。可能是测试接近饱和了，也可能是剩下的问题需要另一种能力，比如长时间探索、使用工具，或者从失败中总结经验。

更有说服力的判断，是把资源控制住：同样的数据、算力和交互次数，模型学会一个新任务需要多少样本？学到的东西能不能迁移到其他任务？遇到错误之后，下一次能不能真正做得更好？然后再看，增加资源时，这些指标是不是还在稳定改善。

所以我不会仅凭某一代模型让人感觉没有那么惊艳，就判断进步变慢了。我们需要先明确衡量的是哪一种学习，再看它在相同条件下的效率，以及规模扩大之后的收益。尤其是对于 agent，我会更关心它能不能把实际交互中的经验变成后续能力的提升。

r001.rationale: The response discusses measuring sample efficiency and improvement, but does not say the researcher feels less ingenuity is now needed to get models to learn a task.

r002.rationale: It mentions interaction and agent experience as ways to improve, but does not identify environments as a form of learning data.
